Adult Rough-head sea catfish Carlarius latiscutatus reach a formidable total length, with the largest recorded individuals attaining 85 centimeters [Li = 85 centimeters], placing this species among the larger ariids inhabiting West African coastal waters. Sexual maturity, however, occurs at a considerably smaller body size; field surveys indicate that puberty is achieved at a total length of 27.5 centimeters [Lp = 27.5 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a distinct shift in reproductive physiology. Upon reaching this length, the gonads begin vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis, marking the transition from a juvenile, non-reproductive state to that of a potential spawning adult. The size at maturity, when expressed as a proportion of the ultimate length, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive investment relative to the species’ maximum attainable size, a pattern observed in several other tropical ariid catfishes.

Neonatal mass in Carlarius latiscutatus is remarkably low, with freshly eclosed yolk-sac larvae weighing only 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a direct consequence of the modest diameter of the fertilized ova. The egg itself measures approximately 1.5 millimeters in diameter, and the tiny prolarvae that emerge from the chorion are heavily reliant on their endogenous yolk reserves during the initial lecithotrophic phase. This minuscule starting mass necessitates a period of rapid exogenous feeding once the mouth opens and the yolk sac is fully resorbed, as larvae must quickly accumulate somatic tissue to survive the high predation pressures typical of estuarine nursery grounds. At the onset of exogenous feeding, the larvae have a body mass of merely 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a value that illustrates the altricial condition of the species' early life stages and the stark contrast with the eventual adult mass of roughly 6500 grams [Wwi = roughly 6500 grams].

The production of offspring in this species is tightly linked to thermal conditions, occurring maximally at a water temperature of 9.4 °C [T = 9.4 °C]. Under these cool, stable temperatures, a reproducing female produces approximately 90 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 90 eggs per clutch], and females are capable of yielding roughly one such clutch per day [F_R_i = roughly one such clutch per day] during the peak of the spawning season. This intense daily output, sustained over the reproductive window, allows for a remarkable cumulative fecundity. The combination of a moderate clutch size with an extremely short inter-clutch interval represents a high-gain reproductive tactic that may compensate for elevated rates of egg and larval mortality in the variable coastal environments the species inhabits. Producing eggs at 9.4 °C [T = 9.4 °C] appears to optimize the trade-off between maternal metabolic expenditure and the developmental viability of the yolked oocytes.

As individuals progress from the juvenile stage toward reproductive participation, body mass increases dramatically. The wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the 27.5 centimeter length threshold, is approximately 206.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 206.3 grams], a mass that reflects the accumulation of muscle and skeletal tissue necessary for successful foraging and predator avoidance. By the time a fish has reached its asymptotic body size, somatic growth is essentially complete, and the ultimate wet weight stabilizes at roughly 6500 grams [Wwi = roughly 6500 grams]. This order-of-magnitude increase in body mass between the pubertal and ultimate stages highlights a prolonged period of post-maturation somatic expansion, a characteristic feature of indeterminate growers. Attaining an ultimate wet weight of 6500 grams [Wwi = 6500 grams] enables this ariid to exploit a broader trophic niche than smaller sympatric species, given the direct relationship between body mass and gape width in predatory teleosts.

Longevity data for Carlarius latiscutatus, gathered from tag-recapture studies and validated by otolith annuli counts, indicate a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] when the fish are maintained at an ambient water temperature of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C]. This decadal lifespan is typical for a marine catfish of its body size, reflecting a pace of life that includes a multi-year juvenile phase, several reproductive seasons as a spawning adult, and eventual senescence marked by reduced feeding activity and slower annual growth increments. In warmer waters, metabolic demands are elevated, and the 10-year lifespan (10 years) [am = 10 years] recorded at 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C] may represent the upper bound of physiological durability under natural conditions. Older individuals, particularly those beyond eight years, exhibit worn dentition and a higher incidence of parasitic load, suggesting that senescent deterioration imposes a functional limit on feeding efficiency before organismal death occurs.
